# Milvus Lite Version Skew Corrupts the memsearch Index

On 2026-10-10 the `daily-backup` job failed its `memsearch-index:full-set` step with the error "database was made by an older Milvus Lite version." Seventy-one other jobs completed; only the index step failed, and an independently running index process (pid 44870) ran ~29 minutes before exiting with the same error. The chosen remedy was to move `~/.memsearch/milvus.db` aside as `milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10` and rebuild from scratch, on the grounds that the index is derived from markdown notes and therefore loses nothing. The rebuild indexed 14,614 chunks and exited 0.

## Key Points

- **The failure is version skew in a local database file, not corruption of source data.** A Milvus Lite upgrade left an on-disk database the new library refuses to open, and because the index is derived from markdown notes, discarding and rebuilding is the cheapest correct fix.
- **Move aside rather than delete.** The old database was renamed `milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10`, keeping a rollback path and a dated record of what the pre-upgrade state was. An earlier plan named it `milvus.db.bak-2026-10-10`; the `.pre-3x-` form is what was actually run.
- **A rebuild must cover the full path set.** A partial path set is destructive — indexing a subset deletes previously indexed data. The full set is 13 paths, of which 12 exist (`~/.codex/memories` does not), and this constraint was already recorded in memory.
- **Two concurrent index runs contend for the same database lock,** so a duplicate run has to be stopped and the existing one allowed to finish; this is the same lock-contention signature previously seen as an exit-1 after a long wait.
- **The `dcg` guard blocked the agent's own `mv` of a path under `~`,** so the move had to be run by the user with a `!` prefix; separately, the guard blocked shell-variable redirects, and literal absolute paths in the memsearch invocation passed. No `settings.json` change was made.
- **Verification is a positive log line, not the absence of an error:** confirm the next `daily-backup` run (or a hand run of `daily-backup.ps1`) shows the `INDEX full set` step passing before archiving and clearing `.errors.log`. As of the 21:52 closeout this verification had not yet happened, and the error log still carried 7 entries.
- **The backup's own exit code is not evidence the SSD leg ran.** A parallel session recorded that `status: OK` does not establish the CRASHBOX volume was mounted and copied — the check is the receipt file at `/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup/_receipts/run-*.txt`, because rsync preserves source mtimes and so `ls -la` or `du` on the destination shows week-old dates even after a perfect capture.

## Details

This is a textbook instance of install-time environment capture rotting: a library upgrade changed the reader while the written artifact stayed at the old format, and nothing surfaced until a scheduled job happened to touch it. What makes the diagnosis tractable is the derived/primary distinction — the Milvus database holds no information that does not exist in the markdown notes it was built from, so the decision tree collapses to "rebuild" rather than "migrate" or "recover." Recognizing that an artifact is regenerable is what licenses the destructive-looking move; the same reasoning that made interim publication cheap in the open-data case applies here to deleting four hours of indexing work. The rename rather than delete is still worth the keystrokes, because it costs nothing and preserves the ability to answer "what did the old file actually contain" if the rebuild turns out to have missed a path.

Two operational hazards surfaced around the rebuild rather than in it. The first is that the rebuild's correctness depends on its argument list: memsearch treats the supplied path set as authoritative, so indexing a subset silently drops everything outside it. That turns a convenient "just reindex the one folder that changed" into a data-loss operation, and it is why the full 13-path list (12 existing) was reconstructed from memory before the run. The second is lock contention. Two index processes against one database produce a stall whose externally visible form — a long wait, then a nonzero exit — is indistinguishable from a crash, which is exactly the signature previously catalogued for `memsearch-drain.ps1`. The correct first check on a long-running index is therefore "is another run already holding the lock," not "is the code broken."

The `dcg` guard's behavior is worth recording precisely because the session chose not to weaken it. The guard refuses any agent-issued `mv` of a path under the home directory and refuses shell-variable redirects, which meant the single necessary move had to be handed to the user as a `!`-prefixed command — the narrowest-sufficient escalation rather than a settings edit. The agent initially proposed relaxing the guard for the one move and then abandoned that route when it proved unnecessary. Literal absolute paths inside the memsearch call were accepted, which is the workaround that kept the rebuild itself agent-runnable. No change was made to `settings.json`, keeping the guard intact for every subsequent session; this is the same posture taken when a dcg rule blocked branch deletion and a multi-repo status loop.

A final verification lesson arrived from a concurrent stack-health session on the same evening. That session deferred the Milvus rebuild in favour of fixing git divergence and a full `MEMORY.md`, and in the process established that the nightly backup's `OK` status says nothing about whether the SSD leg actually ran — the receipt file under `/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup/_receipts/` is the only artifact that dates the capture, because rsync's mtime preservation makes the destination directory listing look stale regardless. That is the same shape as the index failure itself: a status field whose scope is narrower than the question being asked of it, answered correctly only by finding the artifact that the operation authored.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/memsearch-indexing-lock-docker-dependency]] — The prior lock-contention and Docker/Milvus dependency findings; this article adds the version-skew failure mode and the full-path-set constraint.
- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The accumulated catalogue of memsearch failure causes this extends.
- [[concepts/shutdown-induced-dlopen-failure-false-alarm]] — The complementary case where memsearch was never broken at all, making cause classification the first step.
- [[concepts/dcg-guard-false-positives-native-tool-workaround]] — The guard that blocked the `mv` and the shell-variable redirect, plus the escape hatches that worked.
- [[connections/narrowest-sufficient-escalation-over-blanket-bypass]] — Why a one-off `!` command was preferred over relaxing the guard in `settings.json`.
- [[connections/install-time-environment-capture-rots-silently]] — The general class: a host fact (library version) frozen at write time, detected only when something reads the artifact.
- [[concepts/clear-the-error-log-only-after-a-clean-run]] — Why `.errors.log` stays until the backup's `INDEX full set` line passes; still unverified at the day's close.
- [[concepts/backup-status-ok-versus-job-count]] — The companion case where the backup's summary field is narrower than the coverage question; the receipt file is the SSD-leg equivalent of the job-count tell.
- [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]] — Why `status: OK` and a destination mtime both answer a narrower predicate than "did the SSD copy happen."
- [[connections/an-error-names-the-transport-not-the-cause]] — The rebuild log's connection timeouts naming a layer rather than a cause.
- [[connections/write-the-expensive-stage-to-disk-before-the-fragile-one]] — The derived-artifact boundary that made the rebuild safe.

Closeout session (21:52): error log still at 7 entries, clearing deferred until the underlying fixes are confirmed.

# Consolidating a Full MEMORY.md Without Losing Facts

On 2026-10-10 a stack-health session found `MEMORY.md` at 2,491 of its 2,500-character cap, which blocked further writes outright. Consolidation brought it to 2,440 — about 60 characters of headroom — with every thread and pointer preserved. The stated rule was that parked items remain as one-liners carrying a pointer to their fuller record, so no fact was lost in the compression. The session's own verdict was that the file is "sustainable but fragile," and that the next write will again require either consolidation or migrating parked items out to project repositories.

## Key Points

- **A character cap is a hard write barrier, not a warning.** At 2,491/2,500 the file could not accept new content at all, so relief work became a prerequisite for recording anything else.
- **Compression preserved pointers rather than content.** Each parked item was reduced to a one-liner plus a pointer, which keeps the fact retrievable while removing its prose from the always-loaded surface.
- **Sixty characters of headroom is not relief.** The session explicitly characterised the result as fragile and named the next move — relocating the oldest or stalest parked items into their project `docs/STATUS.md` files — as the only route to lasting room.
- **This is the third recorded instance of the same trim-at-the-cap cycle,** which is the argument for treating relief as the paired half of every Tier A write rather than as a periodic emergency.
- **The hazard of trimming is destroying a fact's only copy,** which is why pointer-preserving compression is the safe form and free-text shortening is not.

## Details

The cap exists because `MEMORY.md` is loaded into every session, so its size is a standing per-session tax rather than a one-time storage cost. That makes the trade-off explicit: content earns its place by being needed at the start of most sessions, and anything that does not meet that bar should live somewhere retrievable instead. Consolidating to one-liners-with-pointers is exactly the move that honours both halves — the memory surface still routes a reader to the right place, but the detail sits in a project file that is only opened when relevant. The same logic drove the memory-index trim from 8,162 to 5,549 characters by rewriting each line to state only *when* to open a file.

What distinguishes this instance is the honest assessment attached to it. Sixty characters is less than one sentence, so the consolidation bought a single write rather than a working margin, and the session said so rather than recording the trim as a fix. The named next step — moving the oldest parked items to their projects' `docs/STATUS.md` — is the structurally correct one, because it changes where the facts live rather than how tersely they are phrased, and because `STATUS.md` is the file a reader arriving at that project will actually open. The alternative, continuing to compress prose at the cap, runs directly into the recorded hazard that a line being trimmed may be a fact's only copy; the discipline is to migrate first and check for a second copy before shortening anything.

# Wait 24 Hours Before Deleting a Session So Backup Captures the Transcript

A 2026-10-10 closeout found 11 sessions finished within the previous 24 hours and judged none of them safe to delete, because the nightly backup had not yet run against their transcripts. The recorded rule is a 24-hour wait before `claude rm`, enforced in practice by `session-sweep.py`, which marks sessions `SAFE TO DELETE` once the condition holds. The same session declined to commit `~/.claude` despite 1,892 dirty files, on the grounds that the transcripts may carry personal data and the Windows sync copies were unreviewed; `~/.claude/global-memory` was pushed separately at commit `927e564`.

## Key Points

- **The deletion precondition is a completed backup, not elapsed session time.** A finished session's transcript exists only locally until the nightly job copies it, so deleting inside that window destroys the only copy.
- **The rule is encoded in a tool, not in memory.** `session-sweep.py` computes the `SAFE TO DELETE` marking, and the discipline is to filter by that marking rather than to eyeball session end times.
- **A large dirty tree is a reason to hold, not to bulk-commit.** 1,892 files in `~/.claude` were held because two distinct unknowns applied — possible personal data in transcripts, and unreviewed cross-machine sync copies — neither of which a single commit could resolve.
- **The holdable and the pushable were separated.** `global-memory` (5 files) was pushed immediately; `~/.claude` was left pending, so the handoff-critical content travelled while the ambiguous content waited.
- **The hold blocked final closeout,** and the session recorded that explicitly as a pending decision rather than resolving it by default in either direction.

## Details

The 24-hour rule is a concrete instance of the general ordering constraint that a durable copy must exist before a local one is removed. What makes it worth encoding in a script is that the operator's intuition points the wrong way: a session that has clearly finished *feels* disposable, and the fact that its transcript is still single-copy is invisible from the session list. `session-sweep.py` closes that gap by computing the predicate the operator cannot see, which is the same reason a backup's job count or receipt file is more informative than its status field. The cost of getting it wrong is asymmetric and irreversible — a deleted transcript is gone, while a session left one extra day costs nothing but a slightly longer list.

The `~/.claude` hold illustrates a different judgement. Committing 1,892 files would have resolved the dirty-tree complaint at the cost of pushing content whose contents had not been examined, in a repository that syncs across machines. Two separate concerns applied: transcripts are a plausible vector for personal data entering a tracked repo, and the Windows sync copies were foreign changes nobody had read. Pushing `global-memory` alone is the correct split, because that repository carries the cross-machine handoff content whose freshness has a real cost, while the undifferentiated transcript bulk does not. Recording the hold as a named pending decision — rather than silently leaving the tree dirty — is what lets the next session resolve it instead of rediscovering it.

# A Stale Session Path Pins Work to the Machine That Created It

A 2026-10-10 session (22:19) found a synced Windows session whose working path pointed at `/Desktop/Dev`, which does not exist on the Mac: the Mac uses `~/DEV` while Windows uses `~/Desktop/DEV`. Because session folders sync between the machines, the unresolvable reference surfaced on the Mac even though the work belonged to Windows. The recommendation was to fix the path on the Windows machine when it is next opened — preserving the work — rather than deleting the session from the Mac, and to leave the Windows laptop otherwise untouched per the standing hands-off preference.

## Key Points

- **Syncing session state does not make it portable.** A session carries an absolute working path, and the two machines place `DEV` differently, so a synced session can arrive at a host where its path cannot resolve.
- **The repair belongs to the machine that owns the path.** The Mac can see the broken reference but cannot fix it correctly; only Windows has the directory the session needs.
- **Deleting is the destructive resolution.** Removing the session from the Mac would clear the symptom and discard whatever work the Windows session held, so stale sessions must be inspected before deletion.
- **The standing hands-off rule applies to the Windows laptop,** so no automated fix was attempted — the action was recorded as a manual step for the next Windows sitting.
- **Symlinks and shortcuts do not reliably bridge the gap,** which is why the durable fix is a host-correct reference rather than a filesystem alias.

## Details

The structural cause is that a session's identity includes a filesystem address, and filesystem addresses are per-machine facts. The repository that syncs sessions faithfully transports the artifact while silently failing to transport the condition that makes it usable — the directory it points at. That is the same asymmetry recorded for synced mods arriving dormant because the enabling environment variable is per-machine, and for a synced API key that works on one host and is untested on another. Sync carries artifacts; it never carries the per-machine state that activates them.

The disposition chosen here follows the ownership rule rather than the convenience rule. From the Mac, two actions were available: delete the unresolvable session, or report it for repair on Windows. The first is locally easy and resolves the visible problem while destroying foreign state; the second costs a carried action item and preserves the work. Acting locally on foreign state is the error mode worth naming, because the local action *succeeds* — the session disappears, the warning stops — and conceals the loss. The same reasoning closed out a Windows-path error entry a few days earlier, where a `C:\Users\...` path in an error log assigned the failure to a machine the Mac could not fix from.

# Flush Outcome Taxonomy: FLUSH_OK, Max-Turns, Version Skew, Session Limit

On 2026-10-10 the memory flush pipeline produced six outcomes across the day: five `FLUSH_OK` results (10:32, 11:22, 11:23, 21:43, 21:52) and one failure at 11:20 reading `FLUSH_ERROR: ResultError: Claude Code returned an error result: Reached maximum number of turns (2) (exit code: 1)`. The max-turns exhaustion is a third distinct failure cause, alongside the previously catalogued SDK/CLI version skew and account session-limit exhaustion, and like them it is identifiable only from the error text.

## Key Points

- **`FLUSH_OK` is the designed null result, not a failure.** Five of the day's six flushes returned it, meaning the flush agent read the conversation and judged nothing durable worth appending to the daily log.
- **"Reached maximum number of turns (2)" is a configuration ceiling, not a defect.** `flush.py` invokes the SDK with `max_turns=2`, so a session whose extraction needs a third turn fails rather than degrading to a partial result.
- **Three causes now share one surface form.** Version skew, session-limit exhaustion, and max-turns exhaustion all arrive as `FLUSH_ERROR` with a nonzero exit code; only the message text distinguishes them, and each calls for a different response (rebuild the pin, wait for reset, or accept the loss).
- **A max-turns failure is the only one of the three that is silently lossy.** Quota and version failures can be retried identically once the blocker clears; a turn-budget failure will recur on the same input, so the session's content is simply not captured.
- **Flush outcomes are per-session and independent,** so a failure at 11:20 followed by `FLUSH_OK` at 11:22 says nothing about the pipeline's health — it says the two sessions had different content.

## Details

The value of the taxonomy is that it separates signals that look identical in `.errors.log` and at session start. A nonzero flush exit always reads as something broken, but the correct response ranges from "do nothing" to "rebuild the environment." Version skew means the bundled CLI has diverged from the system install and needs a `uv lock --upgrade-package` pass. Session-limit exhaustion means the account's quota is spent and the identical retry will succeed after reset. Max-turns exhaustion means the extraction did not fit in the two turns the hook allots, and retrying changes nothing — the only remedies are raising the ceiling or accepting that long or complex sessions occasionally go uncaptured.

That third case is worth recording because it is the quietest. A quota failure resolves itself and a version failure produces a visible, repeated error until fixed; a turn-budget failure produces one line and then the day proceeds normally, with no indication that one session's content is missing from the daily log. Since the daily log is the compiler's source layer, an uncaptured session is a permanent hole in the knowledge base rather than a delayed entry. The `max_turns=2` setting exists to bound per-session cost, so raising it is a real trade-off rather than a free fix — but the loss should at least be legible, which argues for the error text being read rather than the exit code being counted.

The five `FLUSH_OK` results are the complementary point. A pipeline whose correct output is frequently "nothing" needs that output to be distinguishable from silence, which is exactly what the explicit sentinel provides: it records that the check ran and found nothing, rather than leaving an absence that could equally mean the hook never fired. The same reasoning licenses a compile run that produces zero articles as a complete result.

# A Closeout With Nothing to Commit Is a Verification Result

The 21:52 closeout on 2026-10-10 found every `~/DEV` repository already clean and pushed from earlier sessions, made no new commits, and recorded that explicitly: "None this session." Its output was a set of verified negatives — no uncommitted or unpushed work anywhere, registry drift stable at 14 items with no new drift introduced, the landed ledger unchanged at 157 files in the last day, and the 7 `.errors.log` entries confirmed as carried over from prior days rather than newly generated. The session signed off on the judgment that the error log is "informational, not a git blocker." A concurrent closeout on the same evening reached the opposite disposition for `~/.claude`, holding 1,892 dirty files rather than committing them — showing that "nothing to commit" is a per-repository finding, not a global state.

## Key Points

- **A zero-change closeout is a complete result, not a skipped one,** provided the checks actually ran: clean working trees, no unpushed commits, an unchanged landed count, and drift confirmed stable rather than merely unexamined.
- **"No new drift" is a stronger statement than "drift exists."** Holding the count at 14 across a working day establishes that the day's activity did not worsen the registry, which is what makes deferring reconciliation defensible.
- **The error-log entries were classified rather than cleared,** each attributed to a cause outside the harness — the compiler backlog, the memsearch index, `gps-pull` API failures, and the digest send — so none could be closed by a git action.
- **Open decisions were carried forward with owners and counts:** 8 across two repos (6 in `SportScienceResearchRepo`, 2 in `Flint`), covering the concierge pilot, Batch 80, an Evans entry, and interview prep.
- **The 7-day staleness clock was reported per project with ages** — `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` at 1 day, `HPI_Protocol`, `Education_Curriculum`, and `cmj-traffic-light` at 2 days each — converting a vague "these are going cold" into a dated watch list.
- **A clean verdict in one closeout does not generalise across repositories.** The parallel agent-session closeout held `~/.claude` with 1,892 dirty files pending a privacy and sync review, so the day ended with both a clean sign-off and an unresolved hold.

## Details

The value of recording a nothing-happened closeout lies in the difference between a check that ran and found nothing and a check that never ran. The two states are indistinguishable from the absence of output, which is the general failure mode behind reading quiet as health. By stating which repositories were walked, what the landed count was, and that the error entries predate the session, the closeout converts silence into a positive negative result that a later reader can rely on. This mirrors the logic of a compile run that produced zero articles: the backlog was cleared and a dated judgment of "nothing durable" was recorded, which is a different artifact from no compile at all.

The error-log handling is the session's main substantive judgment. Seven entries persisted, and rather than clearing them to silence the session-start banner, the closeout classified each as requiring a fix outside the harness and explicitly declined to treat them as a blocker to signing off. That is the correct resolution of a genuine tension: `.errors.log` functions both as a work queue and as a nag, and clearing it early would have converted a record of unresolved conditions into a record of conditions someone intended to resolve. The same day's selective-clearing precedent — clear fixed entries, keep unfixed ones — is the finer-grained version of this move, but it requires knowing which entries are fixed; here the memsearch rebuild's verification had not yet run, so none qualified.

The staleness and open-decision reporting is the other durable output. Both are lists the session could not act on — a decision has an owner who is not the agent, and a stale project needs a step that is real work rather than closeout work — so the honest disposition is to surface them with enough specificity to be actionable next time. Reporting `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` at 1 day alongside three projects at 2 days is more useful than a count of four stale projects, because the ages say which one will trip the rule first.

A caveat follows from the day's parallelism. Three closeout-flavoured sessions ran at 21:52 against overlapping state, and they did not agree: one found every `~/DEV` repo clean, one held `~/.claude` pending review of 1,892 files, and a third was mid-consolidation on a full `MEMORY.md`. "Nothing to commit" was therefore an accurate report of the repositories that session walked and not a statement about the machine. A clean closeout should name its scope for exactly this reason — the same discipline that keeps a closeout from absorbing another session's work also keeps its clean verdict from overclaiming.

# Connection: Concurrent Closeouts Report on Scopes, Not on the Machine

## The Connection

Three closeout-flavoured sessions ran at 21:52 on 2026-10-10 and reached three different verdicts about the same machine. One walked `~/DEV`, found every repository clean and pushed, and signed off with "None this session." A second found `~/.claude` carrying 1,892 dirty files, declined to commit them, pushed only `global-memory` at `927e564`, and recorded the hold as blocking final closeout. A third was mid-triage on a full `MEMORY.md`, deferred the memsearch rebuild to fix git divergence and the character cap instead, and ended with ~60 characters of headroom and a named next step. Read individually each is correct; read together they describe a day that was simultaneously clean, blocked, and fragile.

## Key Insight

**A closeout's verdict is scoped to what it walked, and the scope is almost never stated in the verdict.** "All repos pushed. Memory captured. Ready for next session" is a true sentence about `~/DEV` and a false impression of the machine, because a sibling session was at that moment holding 1,892 files it had deliberately chosen not to commit. The failure mode is not inaccuracy but overclaim: a clean sign-off reads as global because nothing in its phrasing bounds it.

This is the same defect, viewed from the other side, as the status fields whose scope is narrower than the question being asked of them — a `launchctl` exit code reporting only the last scheduled run, a backup's `status: OK` saying nothing about whether the SSD was mounted. There the field was narrow and the reader generalised; here the report was narrow and the reader generalises. In both cases the repair is to publish the predicate alongside the result: *these repositories, these checks, as of this timestamp*.

Concurrency makes it worse in a specific way. The scope-discipline rule already says a closeout should report rather than repair another session's work, which correctly prevents one session from absorbing another's changes. But the same discipline, applied to reporting, means a session must also decline to speak for state it did not examine — and the clean case is exactly where that restraint is hardest, because there is no visible artifact prompting the caveat. A session that found something to hold writes the hold down; a session that found nothing writes a sign-off.

The practical rule: a closeout's output should name its scope and the count of what it inspected, and a day with parallel sessions should expect its closeouts to compose by union rather than by agreement. The three sessions here compose into an accurate picture — `~/DEV` clean, `~/.claude` held pending review, memory at the cap, memsearch unverified — which no single one of them reported.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-10 (21:52), DEV closeout: "All repos pushed. Memory captured. No blocker to sign off—error log is informational, not a git blocker. Ready for next session."
- 2026-10-10 (21:52), agent-session closeout: "`~/.claude` has 1,892 dirty files… **Pending:** Decide whether to hold or commit `~/.claude` (blocks final closeout)."

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

profile.description: Loads a saved browser profile without saving changes to it.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
